TheAuthors.expansion: C.A.\ Uribe, S. Lee, A. Gasnikov and A. Nedi\'{c}

nodes.name: Iteration complexity of the distributed methods of Nedic et al.
nodes.statement: More recently, in \cite{ned17} new methods were proposed where it was shown that $O((m^2 + \sqrt{L/\mu}m)\log \varepsilon^{-1})$ iterations are required to find an $\varepsilon$ solution to the optimization problem when the function is $\mu$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth, where $m$ is the number of nodes in the fixed undirected network.
nodes.statement_short: Cited rate: $O((m^2+\sqrt{L/\mu}m)\log\varepsilon^{-1})$ iterations for strongly convex smooth distributed problems.
assumptions: $m$ is the number of nodes in the fixed undirected network
conclusions: $O((m^2 + \sqrt{L/\mu}m)\log \varepsilon^{-1})$ iterations are required to find an $\varepsilon$ solution to the optimization problem

nodes.name: Iteration complexity of the unified primal method of Jakovetic
nodes.statement: This newly proposed general method is able to recover existing rates and achieves an $\varepsilon$ precision in $O(\sqrt{L/ (\mu \lambda_2)} \log \varepsilon^{-1})$ iterations, where $\lambda_2$ is the second largest eigenvalue of the interaction matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Cited rate: $O(\sqrt{L/(\mu\lambda_2)}\log\varepsilon^{-1})$ iterations, with $\lambda_2$ the second largest eigenvalue of the interaction matrix.
assumptions: $\lambda_2$ is the second largest eigenvalue of the interaction matrix

nodes.name: Optimal rate of Scaman et al. for distributed optimization
nodes.statement: This new method achieves an $\varepsilon$ precision in $O(\sqrt{L/\mu}(1 + \tau / \sqrt{\gamma}) \log \varepsilon^{-1})$ iterations for \mbox{$\mu$-strongly} convex and $L$-smooth problems, where $\tau$ is the diameter of the network and $\gamma$ is the normalized eigengap of the interaction matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Cited optimal rate combining $\sqrt{L/\mu}$ with network diameter and eigengap.
assumptions: $\tau$ is the diameter of the network and $\gamma$ is the normalized eigengap of the interaction matrix

nodes.name: Distributed convex optimization problem
nodes.statement: Particularly, we consider the following optimization problem \begin{align} \min_{\xb \in \mathbb{R}^n} F(\xb) & \qquad \text{where } \qquad F(\xb)\triangleq \sum\limits_{i=1}^{m}f_i(\xb), \end{align} where each $f_i: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a convex function. Moreover, this problem needs to be solved in a distributed manner where each function $f_i$ is known by an agent $i$ only and agents can interact with other agents over a network.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize the sum of $m$ local convex functions, each known only to its own agent, over a network.

nodes.name: Fixed connected undirected network model
nodes.statement: We model such a network as a fixed connected undirected graph $\mathcal{G} = (V,E)$, where $V$ is a set of {$m$} nodes and $E$ is a set of edges. The network structure imposes information constraints, namely, each node $i$ has access to the function $f_i$ only, {and a node can exchange information only with its immediate neighbors, i.e., a node $i$ can communicate with node $j$ if and only if $(i,j)\in E$}.
nodes.statement_short: Agents sit on a fixed connected undirected graph and communicate only with immediate neighbors.

nodes.name: Laplacian matrix of the graph
nodes.statement: Initially, define the Laplacian matrix $\bar W{\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times m}}$ of the graph $\mathcal{G}$ as \begin{align*} [\bar W]_{ij} = \begin{cases} -1, & \text{if } (i,j) \in E,\\ \text{deg}(i), &\text{if } i= j, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise }. \end{cases} \end{align*} where $\text{deg}(i)$ is the degree of the node $i$, i.e., the number of neighbors of the node.

nodes.name: Communication (interaction) matrix $W$
nodes.statement: Finally, define the communication matrix, sometimes called interaction matrix as $W = \bar W \otimes I_n$, where $\otimes$ indicates the Kronecker product.
nodes.definiendum: communication matrix, sometimes called interaction matrix
differentia: $W = \bar W \otimes I_n$, where $\otimes$ indicates the Kronecker product

nodes.name: Properties of the communication matrix $W$
nodes.statement: One can verify that $W$ is a nonnegative semidefinite matrix, with the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item $W{x} = 0$ if and only if {$x_1 = \hdots = x_m$}. \item $\sqrt{W}{x} = 0$ if and only if {$x_1 = \hdots = x_m$}. \item $\sigma_{\max} (\sqrt{W}) = \lambda_{\max} (W)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $W$ is PSD, its kernel (and that of $\sqrt{W}$) is the consensus subspace, and $\sigma_{\max}(\sqrt{W})=\lambda_{\max}(W)$.

nodes.name: Consensus-constrained reformulation
nodes.statement: Therefore, one can equivalently rewrite the problem in Eq. \eqref{main_problem} as: \begin{align} \min_{\sqrt{W} x=0} {F(x)} & = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{m}f_i(x_i), \end{align} where the constraint $\sqrt{W} x=0$ is equivalent to \mbox{$x_1 = \hdots = x_m$} given that $\ker (\sqrt{W}) = \spn(\boldsymbol{1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the distributed problem as minimizing $F(x)$ subject to the affine consensus constraint $\sqrt{W}x=0$.

nodes.name: Euclidean setup remark
nodes.statement: For simplicity of exposition, we will present our results considering the $2$-norm only, which is called the Euclidean setup. Nevertheless, in Section \ref{sec:discussion} we will point out the generalization to other norms.

nodes.name: $\mu$-strongly convex function
nodes.statement: A function $f(\cdot)$ is a $\mu$-strongly convex function if for any $x,y$ it holds that \begin{align*} f(y) \geq f(x) + \left\langle \nabla f(x),y-x \right\rangle + \frac{\mu}{2}\|x-y\|^2_2, \end{align*} where $\nabla f(x)$ is any subgradient of $f(\cdot)$ at $x$.
differentia: for any $x,y$ it holds that $f(y) \geq f(x) + \left\langle \nabla f(x),y-x \right\rangle + \frac{\mu}{2}\|x-y\|^2_2$

nodes.name: Strong convexity constant of the aggregate function
nodes.statement: Particularly, if each of the functions $f_i(x_i)$ in the problem in Eq.\eqref{consensus_problem2} is $\mu_i$-strongly convex then $F(x)$ is $\mu$-strongly convex, with $\mu = \min\limits_{i=1,\hdots,m} \mu_i$.
assumptions: each of the functions $f_i(x_i)$ in the problem in Eq.\eqref{consensus_problem2} is $\mu_i$-strongly convex

nodes.name: $L$-Lipschitz continuous gradient ($L$-smooth)
nodes.statement: A function $f( \cdot )$ has $L$-Lipschitz continuous gradient if it is differentiable and its gradient satisfies the Lipschitz condition, i.e. for any $x,y$ \begin{align*} \|\nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y)\|_2 & \leq L \|x-y\|_2 \end{align*} A function having $L$-Lipschitz continuous gradient is also referred as $L$-smooth.
differentia: its gradient satisfies the Lipschitz condition, i.e. for any $x,y$ $\|\nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y)\|_2 \leq L \|x-y\|_2$

nodes.name: Smoothness constant of the aggregate function
nodes.statement: If each of the functions $f_i(x_i)$ in the problem in Eq.\eqref{consensus_problem2} has $L_i$-Lipschitz continuous gradients then $F(x)$ has $L$-Lipschitz continuous gradient with $L = \max\limits_{i=1,\hdots,m} L_i$.
assumptions: each of the functions $f_i(x_i)$ in the problem in Eq.\eqref{consensus_problem2} has $L_i$-Lipschitz continuous gradients

nodes.name: Nesterov's Fast Gradient Method
nodes.statement: \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE{Choose $y_0 = x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$} \WHILE{ stopping criteria } \STATE{$x_{k+1} = y_k - \frac{1}{L} \nabla f (y_k)$} \STATE{$y_{k+1} = x_{k+1} + \frac{\sqrt{L \vphantom{\mu}} - \sqrt{\vphantom{L}\mu}}{\sqrt{L}+ \sqrt{\vphantom{L}\mu}}(x_{k+1} - x_k)$} \ENDWHILE \RETURN $x_k$ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Accelerated gradient descent with momentum weight $(\sqrt{L}-\sqrt{\mu})/(\sqrt{L}+\sqrt{\mu})$ for $\mu$-strongly convex $L$-smooth functions.

nodes.name: Initialize iterates
nodes.statement: \STATE{Choose $y_0 = x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$}
nodes.statement_short: Initialize both sequences at the same point.

nodes.name: Main loop
nodes.statement: \WHILE{ stopping criteria }
nodes.statement_short: Iterate until the stopping criteria hold.

nodes.name: Gradient step
nodes.statement: \STATE{$x_{k+1} = y_k - \frac{1}{L} \nabla f (y_k)$}
nodes.statement_short: Take a gradient step of size $1/L$ from the extrapolated point.

nodes.name: Momentum extrapolation
nodes.statement: \STATE{$y_{k+1} = x_{k+1} + \frac{\sqrt{L \vphantom{\mu}} - \sqrt{\vphantom{L}\mu}}{\sqrt{L}+ \sqrt{\vphantom{L}\mu}}(x_{k+1} - x_k)$}
nodes.statement_short: Extrapolate with the constant momentum coefficient.

nodes.name: Return iterate
nodes.statement: \RETURN $x_k$
nodes.statement_short: Return the last primal iterate.

nodes.name: Geometric convergence rate of the Fast Gradient Method
nodes.statement: Specifically it holds for \cref{alg:nesterov} that \begin{align*} f(x_k) - f^* \leq L\left( 1- \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{L}} \right)^k\|x_0 - x^*\|_2^2, \end{align*} where $f^*$ denotes the minimum value of the function $f(x)$ and $x^*$ is its minimizer. This result implies a geometric convergence rate, where one can find a solution that is $\varepsilon$ close to the optimal in \begin{align} N = O\left(\sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}} \log \left( \frac{L\|x_0 -x^*\|^2_2}{\varepsilon} \right) \right) \end{align} iterations.
nodes.statement_short: FGM converges geometrically, needing $O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ iterations for $\varepsilon$ accuracy.
assumptions: $f^*$ denotes the minimum value of the function $f(x)$ and $x^*$ is its minimizer

nodes.name: Optimization problem with linear constraints
nodes.statement: In what follows we will consider a $\mu$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth function $f(x)$ and the general optimization problem with linear constraints \begin{align} \min_{Ax=0} f(x) \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Minimize a strongly convex smooth $f$ subject to the homogeneous linear constraint $Ax=0$.

nodes.name: Lagrangian dual problem
nodes.statement: where the Lagrangian dual problem of Eq. \eqref{main2} is \begin{align*} \max_y \left\lbrace \min_{{x}} \left( f(x) - \left\langle A^Ty,x \right\rangle \right) \right\rbrace. \end{align*} Now, rewrite the Lagrangian dual problem in its equivalent form as a minimization problem \begin{align} \min_y \varphi(y) & \qquad \text{where} \qquad \varphi(y) = \max_x \left\lbrace \left\langle A^Ty,x \right\rangle -f(x) \right\rbrace, \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The dual of the linearly constrained problem, written as minimization of the conjugate-type function $\varphi(y)$.

nodes.name: Strong convexity and smoothness of the dual function
nodes.statement: and $\varphi(y)$ is $\mu_\varphi = \frac{\sigma_{\min}(A)}{L}$-strongly convex in $\ker(A^T)^{\perp}$ and has $L_\varphi = \frac{\sigma_{\max}(A)}{\mu}$-Lipschitz continuous gradients.
nodes.statement_short: The dual inherits strong convexity $\sigma_{\min}(A)/L$ on $\ker(A^T)^\perp$ and smoothness $\sigma_{\max}(A)/\mu$.

nodes.name: Demyanov-Danskin's theorem
nodes.statement: From the Demyanov-Danskin's theorem (see Proposition $4.5.1$ in \cite{Bertsekas2003}) it follows that \mbox{$\nabla \varphi(y) = Ax^*(A^Ty) $} where $x^*(A^Ty)$ is the unique solution to the inner maximization problem \begin{align*} x^*(A^Ty) & = \argmax_x \left\lbrace \left\langle A^Ty,x \right\rangle -f(x) \right\rbrace. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The dual gradient equals $Ax^*(A^Ty)$, the image of the inner maximizer.
assumptions: $x^*(A^Ty)$ is the unique solution to the inner maximization problem $x^*(A^Ty) = \argmax_x \left\lbrace \left\langle A^Ty,x \right\rangle -f(x) \right\rbrace$

nodes.name: Dual-friendly function
nodes.statement: A function $f(x)$ is \textit{dual-friendly} if when considering the optimization problem in Eq.\eqref{main2} one has immediate access to an explicit solution $x^*(A^Ty)$ to the dual subproblem or it can be computed efficiently.
differentia: one has immediate access to an explicit solution $x^*(A^Ty)$ to the dual subproblem or it can be computed efficiently

nodes.name: Minimal-norm dual solution with finite norm $R$
nodes.statement: In general, the matrix $A$ might not be full row rank. Then, the dual problem in Eq.\eqref{dual_problem22} can have multiple solutions of the form $y^* + \ker(A^T)$. If the solution is not unique, we will choose $y^*$ with the smallest norm solution. Moreover, we will denote its norm as $R = \|y^*\|_2$ and assume that $R < \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick the minimum-norm dual solution $y^*$ and assume $R=\|y^*\|_2<\infty$.

nodes.name: $(\varepsilon,\tilde{\varepsilon})$-optimal solution
nodes.statement: We say that a point $\hat x$ is an $(\varepsilon,\tilde{\varepsilon})$-optimal solution for the problem in Eq.\eqref{main2} if the following condition holds \begin{align*} f(\hat x ) - f(x^*) \le \varepsilon \qquad \text{and} \qquad \|A\hat x\|_2 \leq \tilde{\varepsilon}. \end{align*} where $f(x^*)$ denotes the optimal function value the problem in Eq.\eqref{main2}. Moreover note that $\left| f(x^*(A^Ty) ) - f(x^*) \right| \le \|y\|_2\|Ax^*(A^Ty)\|_2 $

nodes.name: Nesterov's Fast Gradient Method on the Dual Problem
nodes.statement: \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE{Choose $y_0 = \tilde{y}_0 =0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$} \WHILE{ $\|y_k\|_2 \|Ax^*(A^Ty_k)\|_2 \geq \varepsilon \text{ and } \|Ax^*(A^Ty_k)\|_2 \geq \tilde{\varepsilon}$ } \STATE{$y_{k+1} = \tilde{y}_k - \frac{1}{L_\varphi} Ax^*(A^T\tilde{y}_k)$} \STATE{$\tilde{y}_{k+1} = y_{k+1} + \frac{\sqrt{L_\varphi} - \sqrt{\mu_\varphi\vphantom{L_\varphi}} }{\sqrt{L_\varphi}+ \sqrt{\mu_\varphi\vphantom{L_\varphi}}}(y_{k+1} - y_k)$} \ENDWHILE \RETURN $y_k$ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Run accelerated gradient descent on the dual, using $Ax^*(A^Ty)$ as the dual gradient oracle.

nodes.name: Initialize dual iterates at zero
nodes.statement: \STATE{Choose $y_0 = \tilde{y}_0 =0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$}
nodes.statement_short: Start both dual sequences at the origin.

nodes.name: Stopping-criterion loop
nodes.statement: \WHILE{ $\|y_k\|_2 \|Ax^*(A^Ty_k)\|_2 \geq \varepsilon \text{ and } \|Ax^*(A^Ty_k)\|_2 \geq \tilde{\varepsilon}$ }
nodes.statement_short: Loop until both the duality-gap surrogate and the feasibility residual are small.

nodes.name: Dual gradient step
nodes.statement: \STATE{$y_{k+1} = \tilde{y}_k - \frac{1}{L_\varphi} Ax^*(A^T\tilde{y}_k)$}
nodes.statement_short: Step along the dual gradient $Ax^*(A^T\tilde y_k)$ with step $1/L_\varphi$.

nodes.name: Dual momentum extrapolation
nodes.statement: \STATE{$\tilde{y}_{k+1} = y_{k+1} + \frac{\sqrt{L_\varphi} - \sqrt{\mu_\varphi\vphantom{L_\varphi}} }{\sqrt{L_\varphi}+ \sqrt{\mu_\varphi\vphantom{L_\varphi}}}(y_{k+1} - y_k)$}
nodes.statement_short: Extrapolate the dual iterate with the $\mu_\varphi,L_\varphi$ momentum coefficient.

nodes.name: Return dual iterate
nodes.statement: \RETURN $y_k$
nodes.statement_short: Return the final dual variable.

nodes.name: Oracle-call bound for FGM on the dual problem
nodes.statement: From \cite{dev12}, we can immediately conclude that the number of oracle calls (calculations of $Ax$ and $A^Ty$) required for the \cref{alg:nesterov2} is \begin{align} N & = O \left( \sqrt{\frac{L_\varphi}{\mu_\varphi}} \log \left(\max\left\lbrace 4 L_\varphi\frac{R^2}{\varepsilon} ,2 L_\varphi \frac{R}{\tilde{\varepsilon}}\right\rbrace \right) \right) = \tilde{O}\left( \sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu} \chi(A^TA) }\right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Dual FGM needs $\tilde O(\sqrt{(L/\mu)\chi(A^TA)})$ oracle calls.
assumptions: the number of oracle calls (calculations of $Ax$ and $A^Ty$) required for the \cref{alg:nesterov2}

nodes.name: Per-agent distributed update equations
nodes.statement: Each node $i$ updates its local variables as \begin{subequations} \begin{align} z_{k+1}^i &= \tilde z_k^i - \frac{1}{L_\varphi} \sum_{j=1}^{m} W_{ij} x^{*}_j(\tilde z_k^j) \\ \tilde z_{k+1}^i &= z_{k+1}^i + \frac{\sqrt{L_\varphi} - \sqrt{\mu_\varphi\vphantom{L_\varphi}}}{\sqrt{L_\varphi}+ \sqrt{\mu_\varphi\vphantom{L_\varphi}}}(z_{k+1}^i - z_k^i) \end{align} \end{subequations} where $W_{ij} = [\bar W]_{ij} \otimes I_n$ and $x^{*}_j(w_k)$ is the components of solution of the dual subproblem shared by agent $j$.
nodes.statement_short: Node-level form of dual FGM after the change of variables $z_k=\sqrt{W}y_k$: each agent mixes only neighbor values.

nodes.name: Theorem (Case 1)
nodes.statement: Assume $F(x)$ is dual-friendly, \mbox{$L$-smooth} and $\mu$-strongly convex. Moreover, set $\tilde{\varepsilon} = \varepsilon/ R$. Then, after \begin{align*} N = O\left( \sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}\chi(W)} \log \left( \frac{\sigma_{\max}(W)R^2}{\mu \epsilon} \right) \right) \end{align*} iterations (oracle calls) of Eqs.\cref{per_agent}, the point $x^*(z_N)$ is an $(\varepsilon,\varepsilon/R )$-optimal solution to the optimization problem in Eq.~\eqref{consensus_problem2}.
nodes.statement_short: For dual-friendly strongly convex smooth $F$, the distributed method needs $O(\sqrt{(L/\mu)\chi(W)}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ iterations.
conclusions: after $N = O\left( \sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}\chi(W)} \log \left( \frac{\sigma_{\max}(W)R^2}{\mu \epsilon} \right) \right)$ iterations (oracle calls) of Eqs.\cref{per_agent}, the point $x^*(z_N)$ is an $(\varepsilon,\varepsilon/R )$-optimal solution to the optimization problem in Eq.~\eqref{consensus_problem2}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (Case 1)
nodes.statement: The desired result follows from the estimate in Eq.\cref{bound_dual}, the definition of $\chi(A^TA)$ and $A = \sqrt{W}$ and $\tilde \varepsilon =\varepsilon/R$.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $A=\sqrt{W}$ and $\tilde\varepsilon=\varepsilon/R$ into the general dual complexity estimate.

nodes.name: Strongly convex regularized function
nodes.statement: For a convex function $f(x)$, we define the strongly convex regularized function $f^\mu(x)$ with regularizer $r^2(x)$ as \begin{align} f^\mu(x) \triangleq f(x) + \frac{\mu}{2}r^2(x). \end{align}

nodes.name: Theorem (Case 2)
nodes.statement: Assume $F(x)$ is dual-friendly, \mbox{$M$-Lipschitz} and $\mu$-strongly convex. Then, after \begin{align*} N = \tilde O\left( \sqrt{\frac{ M^2}{\mu\varepsilon} \chi(W)} \right) \end{align*} iterations (oracle calls) of Eqs.\cref{per_agent} on the regularized dual problem $\varphi^{\mu_\varphi}(y)$, with $\mu_\varphi = \varepsilon / R^2$ and regularizer $\|y\|_2^2$, the point $x^*(z_N)$ is an $(\varepsilon,\varepsilon/R )$-optimal solution to the optimization problem in Eq. \eqref{consensus_problem2}.
nodes.statement_short: For dual-friendly strongly convex $M$-Lipschitz $F$, $\tilde O(\sqrt{(M^2/\mu\varepsilon)\chi(W)})$ iterations on the regularized dual suffice.
assumptions: on the regularized dual problem $\varphi^{\mu_\varphi}(y)$, with $\mu_\varphi = \varepsilon / R^2$ and regularizer $\|y\|_2^2$
conclusions: after $N = \tilde O\left( \sqrt{\frac{ M^2}{\mu\varepsilon} \chi(W)} \right)$ iterations (oracle calls) of Eqs.\cref{per_agent} ... the point $x^*(z_N)$ is an $(\varepsilon,\varepsilon/R )$-optimal solution to the optimization problem in Eq. \eqref{consensus_problem2}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (Case 2)
nodes.statement: Initially, lets construct a regularized dual problem. Then, we have that \begin{align} \min_y \varphi^{\hat\mu}(y) & = \varphi(y) + \frac{\hat\mu}{2}\|y\|_2^2 \end{align} where $\hat\mu = \frac{\varepsilon}{R^2}$. Assume there exists $y_N$ such that \begin{align*} \varphi^{\hat\mu}(y_N) - \varphi^{\hat\mu}_* &\leq \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \end{align*} where $\varphi^{\hat\mu}_*$ is the optimal value of the regularized dual function. Then \begin{align*} \varphi(y_N) - \varphi^* &\leq \varepsilon. \end{align*} where $\varphi^*$ is the optimal value of the dual function. It follows from \cite{gas16b} that the number of oracle calls required to find a $(\varepsilon,\tilde{\varepsilon})$-optimal solution is \begin{align*} O\left( \sqrt{\frac{2L_\varphi(\varepsilon + 2R \tilde{\varepsilon})}{\tilde{\varepsilon}^2}}\log\left(\frac{4L_\varphi \left( \min\limits_{Ax=0}F(x)-\min\limits_x F(x))(\varepsilon+2R\tilde{\varepsilon}\right) }{\varepsilon\cdot \tilde{\varepsilon}^2}\right)\right) \end{align*} Additionally, from Theorem $3$ in \cite{lan17} it follows that \begin{align} R^2 & = \|y^*\|_2^2 \leq \frac{\|\nabla F(x^*)\|_2^2}{\sigma_{\min}(A)} = \frac{M^2}{\sigma_{\min}(A)}. \end{align} The final results follow by the definitions of $\tilde\varepsilon$ and $L_\varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: Regularize the dual by $\frac{\hat\mu}{2}\|y\|_2^2$ with $\hat\mu=\varepsilon/R^2$, apply the cited inexact-oracle bound, and substitute $R^2\le M^2/\sigma_{\min}(A)$.

nodes.name: Construct the regularized dual problem
nodes.statement: Initially, lets construct a regularized dual problem. Then, we have that \begin{align} \min_y \varphi^{\hat\mu}(y) & = \varphi(y) + \frac{\hat\mu}{2}\|y\|_2^2 \end{align} where $\hat\mu = \frac{\varepsilon}{R^2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Add the quadratic regularizer $\frac{\hat\mu}{2}\|y\|_2^2$ with $\hat\mu=\varepsilon/R^2$ to the dual.

nodes.name: Transfer accuracy from the regularized dual
nodes.statement: Assume there exists $y_N$ such that \begin{align*} \varphi^{\hat\mu}(y_N) - \varphi^{\hat\mu}_* &\leq \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \end{align*} where $\varphi^{\hat\mu}_*$ is the optimal value of the regularized dual function. Then \begin{align*} \varphi(y_N) - \varphi^* &\leq \varepsilon. \end{align*} where $\varphi^*$ is the optimal value of the dual function.
nodes.statement_short: An $\varepsilon/2$-solution of the regularized dual is an $\varepsilon$-solution of the original dual.

nodes.name: Invoke the cited oracle-call estimate
nodes.statement: It follows from \cite{gas16b} that the number of oracle calls required to find a $(\varepsilon,\tilde{\varepsilon})$-optimal solution is \begin{align*} O\left( \sqrt{\frac{2L_\varphi(\varepsilon + 2R \tilde{\varepsilon})}{\tilde{\varepsilon}^2}}\log\left(\frac{4L_\varphi \left( \min\limits_{Ax=0}F(x)-\min\limits_x F(x))(\varepsilon+2R\tilde{\varepsilon}\right) }{\varepsilon\cdot \tilde{\varepsilon}^2}\right)\right) \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the cited oracle-complexity estimate for $(\varepsilon,\tilde\varepsilon)$-optimal solutions.

nodes.name: Bound the dual solution norm
nodes.statement: Additionally, from Theorem $3$ in \cite{lan17} it follows that \begin{align} R^2 & = \|y^*\|_2^2 \leq \frac{\|\nabla F(x^*)\|_2^2}{\sigma_{\min}(A)} = \frac{M^2}{\sigma_{\min}(A)}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $R^2$ by $M^2/\sigma_{\min}(A)$ using the cited theorem.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The final results follow by the definitions of $\tilde\varepsilon$ and $L_\varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the definitions of $\tilde\varepsilon$ and $L_\varphi$ to obtain the claimed rate.

nodes.name: Bound on the norm of the dual solution
nodes.statement: Additionally, from Theorem $3$ in \cite{lan17} it follows that \begin{align} R^2 & = \|y^*\|_2^2 \leq \frac{\|\nabla F(x^*)\|_2^2}{\sigma_{\min}(A)} = \frac{M^2}{\sigma_{\min}(A)}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The squared minimal-norm dual solution is at most $M^2/\sigma_{\min}(A)$.

nodes.name: Estimating the unknown strong convexity parameter
nodes.statement: Note that we typically do not know $R^2 = \|y^*\|_2^2$. Thus, we require a method to estimate the strong convexity parameter $\hat{\mu}$ which is challenging \cite{nes07,odo15}. Therefore, we can apply the restarting technique on $\mu$ \cite{odo15}. The payment for that is just an $8$ multiplicative factor in the estimation \cite{iou14}. Similarly, a generalization of the FGM algorithm can be proposed when $L_\varphi$ is unknown \cite{ani17}. The specific details of this generalizations are out of the scope of this paper.
nodes.statement_short: Since $R$ is unknown, use restarting on $\mu$ at the cost of a factor 8.

nodes.name: Theorem (Case 3)
nodes.statement: Assume $F(x)$ is dual-friendly and $L$-smooth convex. Then, after \begin{align*} N =\tilde O\left( \sqrt{\frac{ LR_x^2}{\varepsilon} \chi(W)} \right) \end{align*} iterations (oracle calls) of Eqs.\cref{per_agent} on the dual problem of the regularized function $F^\mu(x)$ with $\mu = \varepsilon / R_x^2 = \varepsilon / \|x^* - x^*(z_0)\|_2^2$ and regularizer $\|x - x^*(z_0)\|_2^2$, the point $x^*(z_N)$ is an \mbox{$(\varepsilon,\varepsilon/R )$-optimal} solution to the optimization problem in Eq. \eqref{consensus_problem2}.
nodes.statement_short: For dual-friendly $L$-smooth $F$, primal regularization gives $\tilde O(\sqrt{(LR_x^2/\varepsilon)\chi(W)})$ iterations.
assumptions: on the dual problem of the regularized function $F^\mu(x)$ with $\mu = \varepsilon / R_x^2 = \varepsilon / \|x^* - x^*(z_0)\|_2^2$ and regularizer $\|x - x^*(z_0)\|_2^2$
conclusions: after $N =\tilde O\left( \sqrt{\frac{ LR_x^2}{\varepsilon} \chi(W)} \right)$ iterations (oracle calls) of Eqs.\cref{per_agent} ... the point $x^*(z_N)$ is an \mbox{$(\varepsilon,\varepsilon/R )$-optimal} solution to the optimization problem in Eq. \eqref{consensus_problem2}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (Case 3)
nodes.statement: We can regularize the primal problem in Eq. \eqref{main2} such that we instead try to solve \begin{align*} \min_{Ax=0} F(x) + \frac{\mu}{2}\|x -x^*(z_0)\|_2^2, \end{align*} with $\mu = \frac{\varepsilon}{R^2_x}$. Additionally, if the minimizer $x^*$ is not unique we will consider it as the closest solution from $x^*(z_0)$, i.e. closest to the initial point of the algorithm. This take us back to the case of \cref{sec:strong_smooth} for which we can conclude that up to logarithmic factor that the number of iterations required is: \begin{align} \tilde{O}\left( \sqrt{\frac{L R_x^2}{\varepsilon}\chi(A^TA)}\right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Regularize the primal to make it strongly convex, then reduce to Case 1.

nodes.name: Regularize the primal problem
nodes.statement: We can regularize the primal problem in Eq. \eqref{main2} such that we instead try to solve \begin{align*} \min_{Ax=0} F(x) + \frac{\mu}{2}\|x -x^*(z_0)\|_2^2, \end{align*} with $\mu = \frac{\varepsilon}{R^2_x}$.
nodes.statement_short: Add $\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-x^*(z_0)\|_2^2$ with $\mu=\varepsilon/R_x^2$ to the primal objective.

nodes.name: Fix the minimizer when not unique
nodes.statement: Additionally, if the minimizer $x^*$ is not unique we will consider it as the closest solution from $x^*(z_0)$, i.e. closest to the initial point of the algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: Select the minimizer closest to the initialization to make $R_x$ well defined.

nodes.name: Reduce to the strongly convex smooth case
nodes.statement: This take us back to the case of \cref{sec:strong_smooth} for which we can conclude that up to logarithmic factor that the number of iterations required is: \begin{align} \tilde{O}\left( \sqrt{\frac{L R_x^2}{\varepsilon}\chi(A^TA)}\right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Case 1 estimate to the regularized problem.

nodes.name: Theorem (Case 4)
nodes.statement: Assume $F(x)$ is dual-friendly and $M$-Lipschitz. Then, after \begin{align*} N = \tilde O\left( \sqrt{\frac{ M^2R_x^2}{\varepsilon^2} \chi(W)} \right) \end{align*} iterations (oracle calls) of Eqs.\cref{per_agent} on the regularized dual problem $\varphi^{\mu_\varphi}(y)$, with $\mu_\varphi = \varepsilon / R^2$ and regularizer $\|y\|_2^2$, of the regularized function $F^\mu(x)$ with $\mu = \varepsilon / R_x^2$ and regularizer $\|x - x^*(z_0)\|_2^2$, the point $x^*(z_N)$ is an \mbox{$(\varepsilon,\varepsilon/R )$-optimal} solution to the optimization problem in Eq. \eqref{consensus_problem2}.
nodes.statement_short: For dual-friendly $M$-Lipschitz $F$, double regularization gives $\tilde O(\sqrt{(M^2R_x^2/\varepsilon^2)\chi(W)})$ iterations.
assumptions: on the regularized dual problem $\varphi^{\mu_\varphi}(y)$, with $\mu_\varphi = \varepsilon / R^2$ and regularizer $\|y\|_2^2$, of the regularized function $F^\mu(x)$ with $\mu = \varepsilon / R_x^2$ and regularizer $\|x - x^*(z_0)\|_2^2$
conclusions: after $N = \tilde O\left( \sqrt{\frac{ M^2R_x^2}{\varepsilon^2} \chi(W)} \right)$ iterations (oracle calls) of Eqs.\cref{per_agent} ... the point $x^*(z_N)$ is an \mbox{$(\varepsilon,\varepsilon/R )$-optimal} solution to the optimization problem in Eq. \eqref{consensus_problem2}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (Case 4)
nodes.statement: Similarly as in the cases above we will use regularization. We will regularize the primal problem with $\mu = \frac{\varepsilon}{R^2_x}$ and then regularize the dual problem too with $\hat{\mu} = \frac{\varepsilon}{R^2}$. Therefore, up to logarithmic factors the \cref{alg:nesterov2} will stop in no more than \begin{align} O\left( \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\max}(A)R^2_x(\varepsilon+2R\tilde{\varepsilon})}{\varepsilon\tilde\varepsilon^2}}\right) \end{align} iterations. Where the estimate in Eq. \eqref{result2_convex} is unimporvable up to logarithmic factors.
nodes.statement_short: Regularize both primal and dual, then apply the dual FGM stopping estimate.

nodes.name: Doubly regularize primal and dual
nodes.statement: Similarly as in the cases above we will use regularization. We will regularize the primal problem with $\mu = \frac{\varepsilon}{R^2_x}$ and then regularize the dual problem too with $\hat{\mu} = \frac{\varepsilon}{R^2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply primal regularization $\varepsilon/R_x^2$ followed by dual regularization $\varepsilon/R^2$.

nodes.name: Conclude with the stopping estimate
nodes.statement: Therefore, up to logarithmic factors the \cref{alg:nesterov2} will stop in no more than \begin{align} O\left( \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{\max}(A)R^2_x(\varepsilon+2R\tilde{\varepsilon})}{\varepsilon\tilde\varepsilon^2}}\right) \end{align} iterations. Where the estimate in Eq. \eqref{result2_convex} is unimporvable up to logarithmic factors.
nodes.statement_short: Derive the iteration count and note it is unimprovable up to logarithmic factors.

nodes.name: Dependency of $\chi(W)$ on the graph topology
nodes.statement: The specific value of $\chi(W)$ and its dependency on the number of nodes $m$ has been extensively studied in the literature of distributed optimization \cite{ned15}. In \cite{ned17b}, Proposition $5$ provides an extensive list of worst-case dependencies of the spectral gap for large classes of graphs. Particularly, for fixed undirected graphs, one can construct a set of weights $W$ for which $\chi(W) = O(m^2)$ \cite{ols14}. This matches the best upper bound found in the literature of consensus and distributed optimization \cite{ore10,liu13,ols14}. As an immediate conclusion it is clear that the form in Eq.\eqref{consensus_problem2} with the constraint described as \mbox{$\sqrt{W}x=0$} should be preferred over the description as $Wx=0$, even though both representation correctly describe the consensus subspace $x_1 = \hdots x_m$. Particularly, when we pick $A = \sqrt{W}$, we have \mbox{$\chi(A^TA) = \chi(W)$} instead of \mbox{$\chi(W^TW) = \chi(W^2) \gg \chi(W)$}. For example for a star graph \mbox{$\sqrt{\chi(W)} = O( \sqrt{m})$}, for complete graphs $\sqrt{\chi(W)} = O(1)$, for path graphs \mbox{$\sqrt{\chi(W)} \sim \text{diam}(\mathcal{G}) = O( m)$}, for regular networks $\sqrt{\chi(W)} \geq \frac{\text{diam}(G)}{\log m}$. We can observe that typically $\sqrt{\chi(W)} $ corresponds to the diameter of the graph $G$ and the square root of the spectral gap of the interaction matrix.
nodes.statement_short: $\chi(W)$ scales like the squared graph diameter, and the $\sqrt{W}x=0$ formulation is preferable to $Wx=0$.

nodes.name: $\varepsilon$-consensus
nodes.statement: Particularly, we will reach $\varepsilon$-consensus if for any $\varepsilon > 0$ \begin{align*} \sqrt{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{{m}} \left(x^i_N - \frac{1}{{m}} \sum\limits_{j=1}^{{m}}{x^j_0}\right)^2} & \leq \varepsilon \sqrt{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{{m}} \left({x^i_0} - \frac{1}{{m}} \sum\limits_{j=1}^{{m}}{x^j_0}\right)^2}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Consensus problem as quadratic minimization
nodes.statement: This problem can be solved by considering the convex optimization problem \begin{align} \min_{{x}} \frac{1}{2} \left\langle {x,Wx} \right\rangle. \end{align} where $W$ is a communication matrix as defined in Section \ref{sec:problem}.
nodes.statement_short: Reaching consensus is minimizing the Laplacian quadratic form $\tfrac12\langle x,Wx\rangle$.

nodes.name: Iteration estimate for reaching consensus
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{thm:case1} provides a direct estimate on the number of iterations required to reach consensus, particularly we need $O(\sqrt{\chi(W)}\log \varepsilon^{-1})$, where we have used the fact that \cref{consensus} is $\sigma_{\min}(\sqrt{W})$-strongly convex in $x_0 +\ker(W)$ and has $\sigma_{\max}(\sqrt{W})$-Lipschitz continuous gradients. Moreover, it follows that this estimate cannot be improved up to constant factors. It is important to remark that the Fast Gradient Method, with $x^i_0 = \tilde y^i_0$, {does respect the information constraints imposed by the network}. That is, each node only requires the computation of the average of its immediate neighbors and aggregation can be performed in a fully distributed manner.
nodes.statement_short: Accelerated consensus needs $O(\sqrt{\chi(W)}\log\varepsilon^{-1})$ distributed iterations, and this is tight up to constants.
assumptions: \cref{consensus} is $\sigma_{\min}(\sqrt{W})$-strongly convex in $x_0 +\ker(W)$ and has $\sigma_{\max}(\sqrt{W})$-Lipschitz continuous gradients
conclusions: this estimate cannot be improved up to constant factors

nodes.name: Optimality of the four convergence estimates
nodes.statement: The estimates presented in the \cref{thm:case1,thm:case2,thm:case3,thm:case4} cannot be improved up to logarithmic factors. Particularly in the smooth cases where $L < \infty$ these estimations follow (up to logarithmic factors) form the classical centralized complexity estimation of the FGM algorithm, where for a $\mu$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth convex problem we require at most \begin{align*} O\left( \sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu} }\log \left( \frac{\mu R_x^2}{\varepsilon}\right) \right) \end{align*} oracle calls and for a $L$-smooth convex problem we require at most \begin{align*} O\left( \sqrt{\frac{LR_x^2}{\varepsilon}}\right) . \end{align*} oracle calls. In addition to these centralized estimates we need to take into account the fact that one has to perform $\sqrt{\chi(W)} \log (\varepsilon^{-1})$ additional consensus steps at each iteration of the classical FGM.
nodes.statement_short: The four rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors: centralized FGM lower bounds times $\sqrt{\chi(W)}$ consensus steps.
conclusions: The estimates presented in the \cref{thm:case1,thm:case2,thm:case3,thm:case4} cannot be improved up to logarithmic factors

nodes.name: Non-accelerated power-method consensus rate
nodes.statement: The Laplacian matrix $\bar W$ can be written as $\bar W = D - \tilde{A}$ where $\tilde{A}$ is the adjacency matrix of the graph $\mathcal{G}$ and $D$ is the degree matrix. In addition, $\tilde{A} = D P$ for a stochastic matrix $P$ (the transition matrix of a Markov Chain). Thus, one can apply a simple power method such as $x^{k+1} = Px^k$ to find the consensus value (see ergodic theorem for Markov Chains). Each node depends only on the computation of averages of its neighbor values because of the matrix-vector multiplication $Px^k$. As a result the number of required iterations is $O(\chi(W)\log \varepsilon^{-1})$ (\cite{ned09,tsi84,ber89}). This result can be considered as a non-accelerated weighted gradient method for the problem in Eq.~\eqref{consensus} and holds even if the graph is time-varying and directed (i.e. $\tilde{A}$ is not symmetric \cite{ned13,ned15b,ned16}).
nodes.statement_short: The power method $x^{k+1}=Px^k$ reaches consensus in $O(\chi(W)\log\varepsilon^{-1})$ iterations, even for time-varying directed graphs.
assumptions: $\bar W = D - \tilde{A}$ where $\tilde{A}$ is the adjacency matrix of the graph $\mathcal{G}$ and $D$ is the degree matrix
$\tilde{A} = D P$ for a stochastic matrix $P$ (the transition matrix of a Markov Chain)
conclusions: the number of required iterations is $O(\chi(W)\log \varepsilon^{-1})$

nodes.name: Accelerated consensus rates for directed graphs
nodes.statement: However, it is still an open question whether one can get accelerated rates as those provided by \cref{alg:nesterov2} when the graph is directed.

nodes.name: Separability of the dual subproblem
nodes.statement: Note that the dual subproblem can also be computed in a distributed manner. Specifically, we have that \begin{align*} \argmax_x \left\lbrace \left\langle A^Ty,x \right\rangle -f(x) \right\rbrace & = \argmax_{x_i, i=1,\hdots,m} \left\lbrace \left\langle \sum_{j=1}^{m} A^T_{ij }y_j,x_i \right\rangle -f_i(x_i) \right\rbrace. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The dual subproblem splits across agents, each maximizing its own local term.
nodes.section: 6 No Explicit Dual Solution is available

nodes.name: Complexity of solving the auxiliary dual subproblem
nodes.statement: When the function is strongly convex and smooth, we can solve the auxiliary problem in $O\left( \sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}} \log(\delta^{-1})\right) $ oracle calls (oracle call is the calculation of $\nabla f(x)$). On the other hand, when the function is only smooth, we require $O\left( \sqrt{ \frac{LR_x^2}{\varepsilon} }\log (\delta^{-1})\right)$ iterations. Both estimates are optimal up to logarithmic factor. Therefore, in those cases, we propose totally optimal methods.
nodes.statement_short: The inner subproblem costs $O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log\delta^{-1})$ (strongly convex smooth) or $O(\sqrt{LR_x^2/\varepsilon}\log\delta^{-1})$ (smooth) gradient calls.
assumptions: When the function is strongly convex and smooth
when the function is only smooth
conclusions: we can solve the auxiliary problem in $O\left( \sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}} \log(\delta^{-1})\right) $ oracle calls
nodes.section: 6 No Explicit Dual Solution is available

nodes.name: Nesterov smoothing of the dual indicator
nodes.statement: Moreover, by using the bound in Eq. \eqref{Soomin_bound}, we can replace the function \begin{align*} G(Ax) = \max_y \left\langle y,Ax\right\rangle \end{align*} by \begin{align*} G_\varepsilon(Ax) = \max_y \left\lbrace \left\langle y,Ax \right\rangle - \frac{\varepsilon}{2R^2} \|y\|_2^2\right\rbrace = \frac{R^2}{2\varepsilon} \|Ax\|_2^2. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Replace the exact penalty $G(Ax)$ by its smoothed version $\frac{R^2}{2\varepsilon}\|Ax\|_2^2$.
nodes.section: 6 No Explicit Dual Solution is available

nodes.name: Smoothness of the smoothed penalty $G_\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: Finally, one can show that the function $G_\varepsilon(Ax)$ has a $\frac{\sigma_{\max}(A^T)R^2}{\varepsilon}$-Lipschitz continuous gradient, (note that $\sigma_{\max}(A^T) = \sigma_{\max}(A)$).
conclusions: the function $G_\varepsilon(Ax)$ has a $\frac{\sigma_{\max}(A^T)R^2}{\varepsilon}$-Lipschitz continuous gradient
nodes.section: 6 No Explicit Dual Solution is available

nodes.name: Composite smooth/non-smooth problem
nodes.statement: So, we can solve the composite type mixed smooth/non-smooth type problem \begin{align} \min_{\|x\|_2 \leq R_x } \underbrace{G_\varepsilon(Ax)}_{\sim \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\text{-Lipschitz gradient}} + \underbrace{f(x)}_{M-\text{Lipschitz}} \end{align} where gradient oracle for $G_\varepsilon(Ax)$ requires a constant number of $Ax$ multiplications (because we can explicitly write the formula for $\nabla G_\varepsilon (z)$) and the gradient oracle for $f(x)$ requires one $\nabla f(x)$ calculations.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize the sum of the smoothed penalty and the non-smooth $f$ over a ball of radius $R_x$.
nodes.section: 6 No Explicit Dual Solution is available

nodes.name: Complexity of Lan's accelerated gradient sliding
nodes.statement: Using Lan's accelerated gradient sliding \cite{lan16}, one can find an $\varepsilon$-solution (in function value) of Eq. \eqref{composite} without any auxiliary dual problem, after \begin{align*} N_{Ax} &= O\left( \sqrt{\frac{\frac{\sigma_{\max}(A)R^2}{\varepsilon}R_x^2}{\varepsilon}} \right) = O\left( \sqrt{\frac{M^2R_x^2}{\varepsilon^2} \chi(A^TA)}\right) \end{align*} oracle calls, i.e., $Ax$ multiplications and \begin{align*} N_{\nabla f(x)} &= O\left( \frac{M^2 R_x^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right) \end{align*} oracle calls, i.e., $\nabla f(x)$-gradient calculations. Unfortunately, in this approach we can guarantee $\|Ax_N\|\leq \frac{\varepsilon}{R}$ only in the best case \cite{ani15}.
nodes.statement_short: Gradient sliding separates the $O(\sqrt{M^2R_x^2\chi/\varepsilon^2})$ communication calls from the $O(M^2R_x^2/\varepsilon^2)$ gradient calls.
nodes.section: 6 No Explicit Dual Solution is available

nodes.name: Restarted gradient sliding for strongly convex $f$
nodes.statement_short: Restarting extends gradient sliding to strongly convex $f$, giving optimal $\tilde O(\sqrt{(M^2/\mu\varepsilon)\chi})$ communications and $O(M^2/\mu\varepsilon)$ gradients.
nodes.section: 6 No Explicit Dual Solution is available

nodes.name: Proximal-friendly function
nodes.statement: We will say the function $f(x)$ is \textit{proximal-friendly}, if we can solve the auxiliary strongly convex problem \begin{align*} \text{prox}_{f,A^Ty} (z) & = \argmin_x \left\lbrace f(x) + \left\langle y,Ax \right\rangle + \frac{1}{2}\|x-z\|_2^2\right\rbrace \end{align*} explicitly, similarly as the definition of \textit{dual-friendly}.
differentia: we can solve the auxiliary strongly convex problem $\text{prox}_{f,A^Ty} (z) = \argmin_x \left\lbrace f(x) + \left\langle y,Ax \right\rangle + \frac{1}{2}\|x-z\|_2^2\right\rbrace$ explicitly
nodes.section: 7 Acceleration when $f(x)$ is a proximal-friendly functional

nodes.name: Saddle-point complexity with a proximal oracle
nodes.statement: Therefore, given that \begin{align*} \|\nabla G(y',z') - \nabla G(y,z) \|_2 & \leq L_y\|y' - y\|_2 +L_z\|z' - z\|_2 , \end{align*} one can find an $\varepsilon$- solution (in terms of the duality gap) of the saddle point problem \begin{align*} \max_{\|y\|_2\leq R} \min_z G(y,z) \end{align*} after $N_{Ax} = O\left( \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right) $, $Ax$ multiplications, see \cite{bub15}, section $5.2$.
nodes.statement_short: The saddle-point formulation is solved to $\varepsilon$ duality gap in $O(1/\varepsilon)$ communications.
conclusions: one can find an $\varepsilon$- solution (in terms of the duality gap) of the saddle point problem $\max_{\|y\|_2\leq R} \min_z G(y,z)$ after $N_{Ax} = O\left( \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right) $, $Ax$ multiplications
nodes.section: 7 Acceleration when $f(x)$ is a proximal-friendly functional

nodes.name: No acceleration from the naive proximal approach
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, this does not provide any acceleration. Since, to find $\text{prox}_{f,A^Ty}(z)$ typically, one has to find an $\varepsilon$-solution of a strongly convex optimization problem. This can be done in $O(\frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ calculations of $\nabla f(x)$. So the total number of iterations will be of the order $N_{\nabla f(x)} = O\left( \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\right) $.
nodes.statement_short: The naive proximal saddle-point route costs $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ gradient calls, so nothing is gained.
nodes.section: 7 Acceleration when $f(x)$ is a proximal-friendly functional

nodes.name: Proximal dual reformulation of the constrained problem
nodes.statement: Now, let us propose another approach, consider the original problem in Eq. \eqref{main2} and add the additional term $\frac{1}{2}\|Ax\|_2^2$ which is identically zero on any feasible point $Ax=0$. Thus, \begin{align*} \min_{Ax=0} f(x) & = \min_{Ax=0} \left\lbrace f(x) + \frac{1}{2}\|Ax\|_2^2\right\rbrace \\ & = \min_{x,z;Ax=Az} \left\lbrace f(x) + \max_y \left\langle -y,Az \right\rangle + \frac{1}{2}\|Ax\|_2^2 \right\rbrace \\ & =\min_{x,z} \left\lbrace f(x) + \max_y \left\langle -y,Az \right\rangle + \max_{y'} \left\langle y',Az-Ax \right\rangle + \frac{1}{2}\|Ax\|_2^2 \right\rbrace \\ & = - \min_{y,y'} \left\lbrace \max_x \left( \left\langle A^Ty',x \right\rangle -f(x)\right) +\max_{u \in \text{Im}A} \left\lbrace \left\langle y-y',u \right\rangle - \frac{1}{2} \|u\|^2_2 \right\rbrace \right\rbrace ^{Az=u}\\ & = - \min_{y,y'} \left\lbrace \varphi(y') + \frac{1}{2}\| \text{proj}_{\ker(A^T)^{\perp} }(y - y') \|_2^2\right\rbrace \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Adding the identically-zero term $\frac12\|Ax\|_2^2$ turns the problem into a two-variable dual with a projection penalty.
nodes.section: 7 Acceleration when $f(x)$ is a proximal-friendly functional

nodes.name: Acceleration via accelerated proximal gradient on the dual
nodes.statement: If $\varphi(y') $ is proximal friendly, we can solve the auxiliary problem (this is the proximal version of the standard dual problem) explicitly, then using accelerated proximal gradient descent (in the space of $y$) one can find an $\varepsilon$ solution to the dual problem in $ O\left( \varepsilon^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) $ proximal steps \cite{par14}. Moreover, the results in \cite{lin15} allows for an extension to randomized methods. Therefore, we obtain acceleration.
nodes.statement_short: When $\varphi$ is proximal friendly, accelerated proximal gradient reaches $\varepsilon$ accuracy in $O(\varepsilon^{-1/2})$ proximal steps.
conclusions: one can find an $\varepsilon$ solution to the dual problem in $ O\left( \varepsilon^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) $ proximal steps
nodes.section: 7 Acceleration when $f(x)$ is a proximal-friendly functional

nodes.name: Laplacian-regularized distributed problem
nodes.statement: To overcome this drawback, we can formulate another regularization for the problem in Eq. \eqref{consensus_problem2} as \begin{align} \min_{\sqrt{W} x=0} F_\alpha (x) & = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{m}f_i(x_i) + \frac{\alpha}{2}\left\langle x,Wx\right\rangle \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Add the Laplacian quadratic $\frac{\alpha}{2}\langle x,Wx\rangle$ to the objective to improve the condition number.
nodes.section: 8 Improving the condition number when $F(x)$ is strongly convex and smooth

nodes.name: Conditioning and complexity of the Laplacian-regularized problem
nodes.statement: Furthermore, the regularized function $F_\alpha$ is $\mu \geq \min \left\lbrace \sum\limits_{i=1}^{m}\mu_i,\alpha \lambda_{\min}(W)\right\rbrace $-strongly convex and has \mbox{$L \leq \left( \max\limits_{i=1,\hdots,m}L_i + \alpha \lambda_{\max}(W)\right) $-Lipschitz} continuous gradient. Moreover, if we set \mbox{$\alpha \simeq \sum\limits_{k=1}^{m}\mu_k / \lambda_{\min}(W)$}, one can solve the problem in Eq. \eqref{better_cond} with relative precision $\varepsilon$ after (see also \cite{ned16w}) \begin{align*} N_{Wx} & =O\left( \left( \frac{\max\limits_{i=1,\hdots,m}L_i}{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{m}\mu_i} + \chi(W)\right) \sqrt{\chi(W)} \log^2(\varepsilon^{-1})\right) \end{align*} communication steps and \begin{align*} N_{\nabla F(x)} = O\left( N_{Wx} \log^{-1}(\varepsilon^{-1})\right) \end{align*} gradient $\nabla F(x)$ calculations.
nodes.statement_short: With $\alpha\simeq\sum_k\mu_k/\lambda_{\min}(W)$ the smallest $\mu_i$ is replaced by $\sum_i\mu_i$ at an additive $\chi(W)$ price.
nodes.section: 8 Improving the condition number when $F(x)$ is strongly convex and smooth

nodes.name: Interpretation of the improved condition number
nodes.statement: This estimate shows that we can replace the smallest strong convexity constant for the sum among all of them, but we have to pay an additive price proportional to the condition number of the graph. Using the regularization technique with $\mu_i = \frac{\varepsilon}{mR^2_{x_i}} = \frac{\varepsilon}{R^2_x}$ one can extend this result to the case where the function is just smooth.
nodes.section: 8 Improving the condition number when $F(x)$ is strongly convex and smooth

nodes.name: Optimal rates for time-varying and directed graphs
nodes.statement: Nevertheless, it is an open problem to show that optimal convergence rates, comparable to those in the centralized case can be achieved for time-varying and directed graphs.

nodes.name: Acceleration of consensus over time-varying graphs
nodes.statement: Nevertheless, it is known that one can accelerate this value to $\sqrt{\chi(W)}\log \varepsilon^{-1}$ for fixed graphs. Whether acceleration is possible for time-varying graphs remains an open question to the best of the authors' knowledge. Such generalization of Nesterov's accelerated gradient method is unknown \cite{nar05,bub15,all14,lin15,tay17,hu17,sun17}.
nodes.statement_short: Whether $\sqrt{\chi(W)}$ acceleration extends to time-varying interaction matrices is unknown.

nodes.name: Fast Gossip Steps and Chebyshev acceleration
nodes.statement: CPUs in these days can read and write from and to memory at over $10$GB per second, whereas communication over $TCP/IP$ is about $10MB$ per second \cite{lan17}. Therefore, the gap between intra-node computation and inter-node communication is about $3$ order of magnitude. Communication start-up cost itself is also not negligible as it usually takes a few milliseconds. Let us consider that one node can calculate $\nabla f_i (x_i)$ (or even calculate $x^*_i(A^Ty)$) in $1$ unit of time and the communication step takes $\tau$ units of time. In case $\tau \gg 1$, in this regime all the results above seem reasonable because we first think of communication steps. However, if $\tau \ll 1$ one should use a method with multiple communication steps. Chebyshev acceleration is suggested in \cite{sca17}, where instead of using the interaction matrix $W$ one can analyze the algorithm with a different one $P_K(W)$. $P_K(W)$ is a polynomial of degree $K$, and its eigengap is maximized with a specific choice based on Chebyshev polynomials. If $K$ is chosen as $\sqrt{\chi(W)}$ then \mbox{$\chi\left( P_{\sqrt{\chi(W)}}(W)\right) \sim 1$}.
nodes.statement_short: When communication is cheap relative to computation, Chebyshev polynomial acceleration of $W$ makes the effective condition number constant.

nodes.name: Generalization to $p$-norms
nodes.statement: The cases when $F(x)$ is convex or strongly convex can be generalized to $p$-norms, with $p\geq 1$ see \cite{ani17}. Particularly, the definitions of the condition number $\chi(\cdot)$ needs to be defined accordingly. Let's introduce a norm \mbox{$\| x\|^2_p = \|x_1\|_p^2 + ... + \|x_m\|_p^2$} for \mbox{$p\geq 1$} and assume that $F(x)$ is $\mu$-strongly convex and $L$-Lipschitz continuous gradient in this (new) norm $\|\cdot \|_p$ (in $\mathbb{R}^{mn}$), see \cite{nes15}~(Lemma 1), \cite{dvu17b}~(Lemma 1) and \cite{nes05}~(Theorem 1).. Thus \begin{align*} \chi(W) = \frac{\max_{\|h\|=1} \frac{<h,Wh>}{\mu}}{\min_{\|h\|=1, h \perp \text{ker}(W)} \frac{<h,Wh>}{L}} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Results extend to $p$-norms once the condition number $\chi(W)$ is redefined via the corresponding Rayleigh quotients.

nodes.name: Intermediate levels of smoothness
nodes.statement:
One can try to generalize this results to an intermediate level of smoothness. That is, try to propose the method for arbitrary H"older parameter $
u \in [0,1]$. For example, one can use Universal Nesterov's method by skipping the adaptation and proper choosing of $\delta(
u,\epsilon)$. This is another way to obtain results in the non-smooth case as a special situation $
u = 0$. In the dual space, we will not have classical strong convexity but just uniform convexity. However, it can be studied by introducing inexact oracle as in \cite{gas15}.
nodes.statement_short: Holder-smooth ($\nu\in[0,1]$) extensions could be handled by the Universal method with an inexact oracle.
